items.title: How Italian Women Claimed Their Place in Modern Society
items.content:
IN IMAGES

How Italian Women Claimed Their Place in Modern Society

Gallerie d’Italia in Milan presents “LIBERE! 1946–2026. Le conquiste delle donne” (FREE! 1946–2026. Women’s Hard-Won Rights), an exhibition curated by Renata Ferri that traces almost eighty years of women’s achievements in Italy, beginning with the vote of June 2, 1946.

 

By Gaia Squarci. Cover Photo by Publifoto Archive, Intesa Sanpaolo

Through photographs from Italy’s major historical archives, the exhibition traces the social and cultural changes that led women toward emancipation. Running through the whole show is a tension between work and leisure, independence and tradition, captured in scenes of factory workers after World War II, office clerks of the economic boom, housewives, women casting their first votes, and girls screaming at a Beatles concert.

Then the focus shifts to the feminist movement and the battles over divorce and abortion, along with a tribute to women who left their mark on Italian culture, science, politics and the arts.

The final section brings together photographs and multimedia works by contemporary women artists. Above all, the show makes clear that rights are never handed out. They were won by earlier generations who fought for them, and they can be lost again at any time.

The exhibition “LIBERE! 1946–2026. Le conquiste delle donne” is on view at Gallerie d’Italia in Milan, Italy, until February 7, 2027.

items.content_es:
IN IMAGES

Cómo las mujeres italianas reclaman su lugar en la sociedad moderna

Gallerie d’Italia in Milan presents “LIBERE! 1946–2026. Le conquiste delle donne” (FREE! 1946–2026. Women’s Hard-Won Rights), an exhibition curated by Renata Ferri that traces almost eighty years of women’s achievements in Italy, beginning with the vote of June 2, 1946.

 

Por Gaia Squarci. Foto de Cubierta por Archivo de Publifoto, Intesa Sanpaolo

A través de fotografías de los principales archivos históricos de Italia, la exposición traza los cambios sociales y culturales que llevaron a las mujeres hacia la emancipación. Correr a través de todo el espectáculo es una tensión entre el trabajo y el ocio, la independencia y la tradición, capturados en escenas de trabajadores de fábrica después de la Segunda Guerra Mundial, secretarios de oficina del boom económico, amas de casa, mujeres emitiendo sus primeros votos, y niñas gritando en un.

Luego el enfoque se desplaza hacia el movimiento feminista y las batallas por el divorcio y el aborto, junto con un homenaje a las mujeres que dejaron su marca en la cultura italiana, la ciencia, la política y las artes.

La sección final reúne fotografías y obras multimedia de artistas contemporáneos. Sobre todo, el espectáculo deja claro que los derechos nunca se entregan. Fueron ganados por generaciones anteriores que lucharon por ellos, y pueden perderse de nuevo en cualquier momento.

The exhibition “LIBERE! 1946–2026. Le conquiste delle donne” is on view at Gallerie d’Italia in Milan, Italy, until February 7, 2027.

items.title: In Santa Fe, One Hundred Photographers and Forty-Five Reviewers
items.content:
Picture a large pavilion, strings of bare bulbs hanging from the ceiling, and long tables covered in white cloth. On them, prints are laid out edge to edge, wooden boxes stand open, and books are propped up like small altars. Behind each table, a photographer waits. In front, visitors lean in, turn a page, ask a question. A reviewer from a major publication stops, then stays. This is the Portfolio Walk, the public face of Review Santa Fe. Each year, the evening draws crowds. CENTER says more than 1,000 people can pass through in a single night.

A professional crossroads

Review Santa Fe is first of all a working conference. One hundred photographers, selected by an independent committee, travel to New Mexico with a project they hope will find a wider audience. There, they sit down with the people who can help it do so.

This year, CENTER welcomes 19 editors, including representatives of National Geographic, The New York Times, Oxford American and NPR. They are joined by 10 museum curators, 7 book publishers and 9 gallery representatives. That makes 45 reviewers, who spend the weekend looking at work and deciding which of it deserves to travel further. The result is nearly 1,000 one-on-one meetings in four days.

Participation is by application. A selection committee of three industry professionals ranks the submitted projects, and invited photographers then pay a fee for their package of reviews. CENTER says scholarships and payment plans are available.

The format reflects CENTER’s own history. Founded in 1994, the Santa Fe non-profit supports socially and environmentally engaged lens-based projects through education, funding and partnerships. Review Santa Fe is its largest event of the year.

Six award and grant recipients

The weekend opens on October 23 at CENTER Gallery with The Conditions of Seeing, an exhibition of the 2026 award and grant recipients: Marcus DeSieno, Anna Mia Davidson, Leonard Suryajaya, Peter Teh, Ville Varumo and Volodymyr Voznyy.

The show gathers landscape, portraiture, staged scenes, diary-like image-making and socially engaged practice. What links them is a question: under what conditions do people, places and selves become visible? Their work looks at how seeing is shaped by political systems, inherited histories, environmental change, cultural assumptions, relationships, memory and care.

On the morning of October 25, Marcus DeSieno, a Project Launch Grant recipient, presents Geography of Disappearance: Migrant Deaths on the US/Mexico Border. The United Nations has described the border as the deadliest land crossing in the world. DeSieno photographs along it, going to the exact places where the bodies of unknown migrants were found. He locates them using autopsy reports and data collected by humanitarian organisations and by local and state police. The photographs, he writes in his project statement, serve “as a space for somber remembrance of the deceased.”

Open to all

Most of the public programme is free. The Portfolio Walk takes place on October 24 and lets visitors speak directly with the hundred photographers. The work covers a wide range of contemporary photography on social, environmental and political subjects. It can be previewed beforehand on the Review Santa Fe Listing website. On October 26, a panel with the reviewers, moderated by Thomas Werner, closes the weekend with a discussion of how photographic projects get published and exhibited.

Online and in-person events are both offered this year.

The Review Santa Fe Photo Symposium takes place from October 23 to 26, 2026, in Santa Fe, New Mexico (USA).  The full programme is on CENTER’s website, and the work of the hundred photographers can be previewed on the Review Santa Fe Listing. Applications for the 2026 edition closed on February 28, and the next call for entry opens in January 2027 on CENTER’s application page.

items.title_es: En Santa Fe, un centenar de fotógrafos y cuarenta y cinco revisores
items.content_es:
Imagínate un gran pabellón, cuerdas de bulbos desnudos colgando del techo, y largas mesas cubiertas de tela blanca. En ellas, las huellas se colocan borde a borde, cajas de madera se abren, y los libros se proponen como altares pequeños. Detrás de cada mesa, un fotógrafo espera. En frente, los visitantes se inclinan, giran una página, hacen una pregunta.

Un cruce profesional

Revisión Santa Fe es ante todo una conferencia de trabajo. Cien fotógrafos, seleccionados por un comité independiente, viajan a Nuevo México con un proyecto que esperan encontrar un público más amplio. Allí, se sientan con la gente que puede ayudar a hacerlo.

Este año, CENTER da la bienvenida a 19 editores, incluyendo representantes de National Geographic, El New York Times, Oxford American y NPR. Se unen a 10 curadores de museos, 7 editores de libros y 9 representantes de galería, lo que hace 45 revisores, que pasan el fin de semana mirando el trabajo y decidiendo cuál de ellos merece viajar más lejos. El resultado es casi 1.000 reuniones de uno a uno en cuatro días.

La participación es por solicitud. Un comité de selección de tres profesionales de la industria clasifica los proyectos presentados, e invitó a los fotógrafos a pagar una cuota para su paquete de opiniones. CENTER dice que las becas y los planes de pago están disponibles.

El formato refleja la propia historia de CENTER. Fundada en 1994, la organización sin ánimo de lucro Santa Fe apoya proyectos basados en objetivos social y ambientalmente comprometidos a través de la educación, la financiación y las asociaciones.

Seis beneficiarios de la concesión de premios y ganancias

El fin de semana se abre el 23 de octubre en CENTER Gallery con Las condiciones de la búsqueda, una exposición de los ganadores del premio 2026: Marcus DeSieno, Anna Mia Davidson, Leonard Suryajaya, Peter Teh, Ville Varumo y Volodymyr Voznyy.

El espectáculo reúne paisajes, retratos, escenas escénicas, creación de imágenes como diario y práctica socialmente comprometida. Lo que los une es una pregunta: ¿bajo qué condiciones se hacen visibles las personas, los lugares y los seres? Su trabajo mira cómo el ver está conformado por sistemas políticos, historias heredadas, cambio ambiental, supuestos culturales, relaciones, memoria y cuidado.

En la mañana del 25 de octubre, Marcus DeSieno, ganador de la beca de lanzamiento de proyectos, presenta Geografía de las desapariciones: Muertes migrantes en la frontera entre Estados Unidos y MéxicoLas Naciones Unidas han descrito la frontera como el cruce más mortífero del mundo. Fotografías de DeSieno a lo largo de ella, yendo a los lugares exactos donde se encontraron los cuerpos de migrantes desconocidos. Los ubica utilizando informes de autopsia y datos recogidos por organizaciones humanitarias y por la policía local y estatal. Las fotografías, escribe en su declaración de proyecto, sirven “como espacio para el recuerdo sombrío de los fallecidos”.

Abierto a todos

La mayor parte del programa público es gratuito. El Paseo de Portfolio tiene lugar el 24 de octubre y permite a los visitantes hablar directamente con los cien fotógrafos. El trabajo cubre una amplia gama de fotografía contemporánea sobre temas sociales, ambientales y políticos. Puede ser presentado de antemano en el sitio web de Revisión Santa Fe Listing. El 26 de octubre, un panel con los revisores, moderado por Thomas Werner, cierra el fin de semana con una discusión sobre cómo se publican los proyectos fotográficos y exhiben.

Este año se ofrecen eventos en línea y en persona.

El Simposio de fotos de Santa Fe se realiza del 23 al 26 de octubre de 2026, en Santa Fe, Nuevo México (USA). Sitio web de CENTER, y el trabajo de los cien fotógrafos se puede prever en el Revisión Santa Fe Listado. Solicitudes para la edición 2026 cerrada el 28 de febrero, y la próxima convocatoria de entrada se abre en enero de 2027 en Página de aplicación de CENTER.

items.title: Olivier Metzger: Taking the Night as It Comes
items.content:
Some photographers light things up. Olivier Metzger looks for what light conceals, and finds it behind a hotel door, a sea-green curtain, the silhouette of Tilda Swinton in an olive suit. Take war as it comes, the French say, “à la guerre comme à la guerre.” Metzger answers in kind: he takes the night as it comes, amber, sodium-lit, haunted by cinema.

Born in Mulhouse in 1973, he first worked as a nurse. Caregiver, then director. At 28 he entered the École nationale supérieure de la photographie (ENSP) in Arles, graduated in 2004 and won the Prix Voies Off at the Rencontres the same year with his series “Data.” Then came Libération, Télérama, Le Monde, The New York Times (assignments, that genre where the subject sets the rules, and the hour too). Metzger slipped a dramaturgy into them, sculpting his images in “a delicate chiaroscuro, often tinged with melancholy.”

David Lynch surfaces quickly in critics’ pieces, and for good reason: in 2012, the filmmaker made the series “Smile (Forever)” his favorite at Paris Photo. A film? A dream? A hotel room? The doubt is maintained, and so is the fiction. Even a doe spotted by chance on a Nevada road (Bambi, Nevada, 2010) enters it like a fairy tale. The world seems about to come apart, and Metzger lights it so that it holds a moment longer. Publisher Actes Sud introduces him as a “photographer of the strange.”

Then came the loss. On November 2, 2022, Olivier Metzger died in a road accident near Arles, his adopted city. In 2023, the Rencontres asked Éric Reinhardt for a tribute. The writer built his text from 49 songs drawn from the photographer’s Spotify library. 49 songs, 49 years. Three years later, the exhibition extends the echo, and the book, published in June 2026 (128 pages), takes the form of a two-voice dialogue fed by the music that accompanied Metzger. One can read it “as a farewell.” Reinhardt, the friend, wants us to feel an artist working “as if he were photographing his own destiny.” Even on assignment.

“Olivier Metzger, Somewhere and Somehow,” is on view at La Croisière, in Arles Arles, through October 4, 2026. The book Somewhere and Somehow is published by Actes Sud and available for €35.

items.title_es: Olivier Metzger: Tomar la noche como viene
items.content_es:
Algunos fotógrafos iluminan las cosas. Olivier Metzger busca lo que la luz oculta, y lo encuentra detrás de una puerta del hotel, una cortina verde del mar, la silueta de Tilda Swinton en un traje de oliva. Tome la guerra como viene, los franceses dicen, "à la guerre comme à la guerre." Metzger responde en especie: él toma la noche como viene, amber, sodium-lit cine.

Nacido en Mulhouse en 1973, trabajó por primera vez como enfermera. Caregiver, entonces director. A los 28 entró en la École nationale supérieure de la photographie (ENSP) en Arles, se graduó en 2004 y ganó el Prix Voies Off en el Rencontres el mismo año con su serie “Data”. Libération, Télérama, Le Monde, El New York Times (Asignaciones, ese género donde el sujeto establece las reglas, y la hora también). Metzger se metió una dramaturgia en ellos, esculpindo sus imágenes en “un delicado chiaroscuro, a menudo teñido con melancolía”.

David Lynch se encuentra rápidamente en las piezas de los críticos, y por buena razón: en 2012, el cineasta hizo la serie “Smile (Forever)” su favorito en Paris Photo. ¿Una película? ¿Un sueño? Una habitación de hotel? La duda se mantiene, y así es la ficción. Incluso una ficha manchada por casualidad en una carretera de Nevada (¿Un sueño?Bambi, Nevada, 2010) entra como un cuento de hadas. El mundo parece estar a punto de separarse, y Metzger lo enciende para que tenga un momento más largo. El editor Actes Sud le presenta como un “fotógrafo de lo extraño”.

Luego llegó la pérdida. El 2 de noviembre de 2022, Olivier Metzger murió en un accidente de carretera cerca de Arles, su ciudad adoptada. En 2023, los Rencontres le pidieron a Éric Reinhardt un homenaje. El escritor construyó su texto de 49 canciones dibujadas de la biblioteca de Spotify del fotógrafo. 49 canciones, 49 años después, la exposición extiende el eco, y el libro, publicado en junio de 2026 (128 páginas),

“Olivier Metzger, en algún lugar y de alguna manera”, está a la vista La Croisière, en Arles Arles, hasta el 4 de octubre de 2026. El libro En algún lugar y de alguna manera es publicado por Actes Sud y disponible por €35.

items.title: Herb Ritts, Greg Gorman, Matthew Rolston: The God-Makers of the City of Angels
items.content:
In 1978, Herb Ritts photographed his friend Richard Gere, then an unknown actor, in a tank top, arms raised, muscles taut. Out of that chance session came a portrait that would help forge his status as a sex symbol: something carnal and animal emanates from it, a raw physical presence sharpened by the oblique, sovereign light of California.

Greg Gorman, trained in cinematography at the University of Southern California, and Matthew Rolston, discovered by the artist Andy Warhol while still a student at the ArtCenter College of Design in Pasadena, moved in the same creative circles as Herb Ritts, those of a Hollywood in full reinvention. Beyond that community, the three artists shared a singular gift: the ability to turn virtually any individual into an icon.

To do this, they applied to photography codes as old as art history itself. Court painters relied on costume; religious painters, on light and scale. Herb Ritts photographed the Irish singer Sinead O’Connor with her head tipped back, her shaved skull offered to the light like a sacrament. The photographer liked to strip his subjects of every superfluous ornament to reveal the archetype beneath, treating light like a chisel.

Gorman, for his part, worked close to his subjects: his black-and-white images, tight, intimate, and shadowed, hunted for the spark particular to each gaze, as in his portrait of a young Leonardo DiCaprio. Rolston, meanwhile, built sets, chose costumes with exacting care, and composed each image by invoking precise pictorial and cinematic references, elevating the portrait to the rank of a small theater, or a film dressing room. Under his lens, a fifteen-year-old Drew Barrymore, her hair cropped short and slicked back, dressed androgynously, recalls the features of a young Elvis Presley.


Vogue and Vanity Fair‘s design director, Charles Churchward, named this constellation “The School of Los Angeles,” noting that their rise “marked a significant shift in the imaging of celebrity.” Matthew Rolston shares that intuition. As he told Print magazine: “I think glamour — and glamour photography — is a substitute for god and goddess worship. The altar is the photo studio. So the goddess comes to the dressing room like she would’ve come to the preparation chamber of a temple. She’s anointed with oils and potions — that would be the hair and makeup team. It is really the same thing.”

Andy Warhol, the founder of Interview magazine, played the role of go-between in this story. Upon discovering, within its pages, Matthew Rolston’s photo essay on a new generation of Hollywood actors, the inventor of Pop Art wrote in his diary: “Matthew is our best photographer now.” Greg Gorman, for his part, made one of the most striking portraits of Warhol himself: tightly framed, in opaque black sunglasses, his white hair haloed around his head, the New York artist appears as impenetrable there as the celebrities in his own silkscreens.

Magazine covers, album sleeves, music videos, films. The images of Herb Ritts, Greg Gorman, and Matthew Rolston coursed through the visual culture of an entire generation raised on MTV. Rolston traces that lineage himself: “Andy Warhol and Helmut Newton were the architects of the postmodern revival of Hollywood glamour.” Immortalized by Herb Ritts, Cindy Crawford, leaning over k.d. lang in a barber’s chair, her face lathered in shaving cream, moves in for a kiss.

This visual language, sensual and meticulously crafted, has long since outgrown California and the confines of photography itself, taken up the world over, even by reality television’s fleeting stars and influencers in the making. Models, after all, are never in short supply. Greg Gorman put it simply: “In my eyes, everybody is interesting; a celebrity, so to speak, in their own right.”

“The School of Los Angeles: Herb Ritts, Greg Gorman & Matthew Rolston” runs from October 1st through November 28, 2026, at the Fahey/Klein Gallery in Los Angeles.

Opening reception: Thursday, October 1st, 2026, 7–9 p.m.

Artist talk: Saturday, October 3rd, 2026, 2–4 p.m.

items.title: Toiletpaper Comes Back for Seconds
items.content:
IN IMAGES

Toiletpaper Comes Back for Seconds

The cult magazine by artist Maurizio Cattelan and photographer Pierpaolo Ferrari makes its return this autumn with Damiani Books, bringing a new issue of images as inventive as they are sharp, and an exhibition in Shenzhen, China.

 

By Guénola Pellen. Photos by Toiletpaper.

The 21st edition of Toiletpaper opens with a cover that conjures Martin Parr’s grotesque vision of summer leisure and the streak of bad taste that is the magazine’s hallmark. An elderly woman photographed from behind, blue swimsuit, pink plastic bag on her arm: her scarlet back reveals, in negative, a smiley face of unburned skin. Maurizio Cattelan, iconoclastic provocateur of the contemporary art world, and Pierpaolo Ferrari, art director whose practice blends fashion, advertising and surrealism, staged every inch of it.

The editorial venture was born of their first collaboration for W Magazine in 2009. “We had so much fun, we said, why don’t we do more of this?” Maurizio Cattelan told The New Yorker in 2011. Toiletpaper launched the following year: not a word, not an advertisement. Every image is built entirely in camera, meticulously staged tableaux vivants with saturated chromatism that subvert the codes of advertising, fashion and cinema.

“We keep homing in on what a Toiletpaper image is. Like distilling a perfume. It’s not about one particular style or time frame; what makes them Toiletpaper is a special twist. An uncanny ambiguity,” Maurizio Cattelan told The New Yorker in the same interview. In this edition, a monkey wrench locks itself around an ear, a fuchsia stiletto brims with a banana split in an equivocal nod to food porn, and a chef’s knife is held upside down, its bare blade turned toward the very hand that brandishes it: chic, precise and sovereignly unsettling.

Published three years after its predecessor, the issue is accompanied by an exhibition at the Fotografiska museum in Shenzhen, China, and a limited-edition 2027 calendar created with German photographer Ellen von Unwerth, high priestess of fashion and glamour photography.

Toiletpaper Magazine 21, by Maurizio Cattelan and Pierpaolo Ferrari, is published by Damiani Books, 40 pages, softcover, $20.

“ToiletFotoPaperGrafiska”, Toiletpaper’s first exhibition in China, runs from October 1st, 2026 to March 14, 2027 at Fotografiska Shenzhen.

items.title: Girls on the Edge of the American Dream
items.content:
IN IMAGES

Girls on the Edge of the American Dream

Belgian photographer Eva Verbeeck traveled across the United States to photograph, with a large format camera, more than four hundred girls between the ages of 8 and 18. America’s Girls, On the Edge of a Dream grew out of the encounter between the image she had as a young girl of the “girl next door” and the true face of America: plural, elusive, impossible to pin down.

 

By Guénola Pellen. Photos by Eva Verbeeck.

Eva Verbeeck grew up in Tessenderlo, a small town in northern Belgium where social life revolved around “a central square with a church, a Monday farmers’ market and a country fair held twice a year.” She found her escape dreaming of America through films, TV shows and comic books. The American girl played the lead role, whether cheerleader, goth, beauty queen or punk at heart.

The artist asked each young woman to bring whatever she is passionate about or finds inspiring. One poses with her horse, another with her electric guitar, a third performs CPR on a training dummy. Many arrive in sportswear. 

The slowness of the large format process creates between them and the photographer “a space of conversation, vulnerability and trust.” Against the digital selfie, instantaneous and carefully curated, these portraits insist on analogue film and the gaze of an outsider looking in.

Uniforms and costumes only tell part of the story: behind the chosen outfits and accessories, the faces, often serious, slip free of any expected role. These moments of intimacy lead the images to “unintentionally describe something touching.” For if, online, photography has become for these girls “a language of projection and wish fulfillment,” the large format camera imposes a truth that escapes all staging.

In Ithaca, a fifteen-year-old swimmer shares with the photographer a personal essay on sexism and feminism. Something shifts: “we cared about the same things and had a responsibility to be heard.” America’s Girls, she adds, is “shaped by the courage and vulnerability of each girl who chose to be seen.” On the edge of the dream, they seem now to be waiting for America to keep its promises.

 




America’s Girls, On the Edge of a Dream by Eva Verbeeck is published by GOST Books (2026).

items.title: Photography and the Music Scene: Listening to the Image
items.content:
In the street, two silhouettes advance, wearing studded belts, sunglasses, leather biker jackets and torn tights. Further on, a couple kiss, their mohawks and tattoos matching. In Dave Clarke’s photographs, on show until the end of September at Jardin21 in Paris, the compositions are raw, the monochromes contrasted, the grain powerful. Nicknamed “The Baron of Techno”, the DJ, producer and remixer has worked with Depeche Mode, The Chemical Brothers and Placebo. He first tried photography in his youth, borrowing his father’s old camera. “But film was expensive, and developing it even more so. So I spent my pocket money on 45s and tapes instead, because you could always ‘develop’ those live, without waiting for a result, or record over them if you got it wrong,” he continues.

An emblematic figure of the techno scene, he draws inspiration from “gothic atmospheres, monochrome punk, soundscapes”, travels to many cities and gladly gets lost on foot. These experiences once again lead Clarke toward visual experimentation, a new way of translating the emotions he feels through sound. But how do the two media feed each other? How do scene photographers manage to impose their aesthetic, their own writing, when they capture the essence of an artist whose work already exists? Passionate about music, Jessica Attia and David Fitt have, like Dave Clarke, made the music scene their favorite space of expression. In the whirl of concerts and festivals, in the studio right beside the performers, or simply around a street corner, they turn composers and their fans into their preferred subjects. They capture an atmosphere, a sensibility, while preserving their singularity. It is a balancing act they have learned to master.

Forging Bonds

“I see my music and my photography as art forms that come together and symbolize my interpretation of the world, my need to try to understand it. I would say music makes me want to shoot, and shooting lets me empty my hyperactive mind. It’s a kind of zen,” Dave Clarke explains. The link between the two media seems obvious to him: “Eyes and ears are connected to the brain, so trying to separate their creative processes almost seems like an oxymoron,” he admits.

For Jessica Attia too, music is a binding thread, a necessary source of inspiration for her visual research. “It is constantly present in my mind and always finds a place in my images,” she confides. A devotee of Polaroid and analog film, the young photographer has already had the biggest names of the scene in front of her lens, among them Billie Eilish, Post Malone and DJ Snake. Their universes differ, yet she approaches every encounter the same way: fully immersed. “I think there is a part of truth, a part of themselves in their music, even if it isn’t the whole of who they are. That is why, as an artist, I have to listen to everything, feel their compositions, understand their creation,” she continues.

It was by “hanging around concerts all the time” that David Fitt made a place for himself in the rock and metal scene. “When I started getting interested in it, a photographer lent me his second camera body so I could experiment. I gave the images to the bands and, little by little, I became known,” he recalls. He often initiates the meetings with the artists he photographs, and considers himself lucky: “I work 90% of the time with people whose music I love,” he says. It is a starting point that allows him to build ties with those he admires. “I feel very privileged to be a collaborator, a fan and a friend to them all at once,” he admits. For him, such prior knowledge is essential: when you are already steeped in an artist’s compositions, it becomes easy to summon them through images.

Letting an Identity Emerge

But how, as a photographer, do you resist the urge to disappear? How do you reconcile two artistic representations? For Jessica Attia, everything comes down to connection: “I want to draw them somewhere they don’t expect to go. That’s where my own vision can take over. If I fully respect their identity, my emotional filter kicks in once we’re in the same room. It’s a kind of sharing: their world and their energy through my prism,” she explains.

David Fitt, for his part, does extensive research, looks at existing visuals, discovers who made them and asks questions to grasp what the band wants. “I also tell myself that if they come to me, it’s so that I make their universe my own,” he admits. He aims to combine the aesthetic of his subjects with his own language. In the end, the pictures fit together like pieces of a puzzle from which a global identity emerges. In Jessica Attia’s work, nearly all the details vanish into the penumbra, chiaroscuros turn abstract, and blurs summon an atmosphere, a mood, rather than a constructed narrative. In David Fitt’s portraits, colored halos set the scene, and enhance or conceal bodies and features. It is a dark, dreamlike universe from which the artists emerge as spectral, almost fantastical figures. “You have to be able to feel the atmosphere visually, or at least the image should show a facet that the music doesn’t give us,” he concludes. “Putting a face to a name makes a project more human, deeper, more compelling, all the more so at a time when AI is sweeping in.”

More information on Dave Clarke, David Fitt and Jessica Attia on their respective websites.

items.title: Global Peace Photo Award: The Hairdryer of Afghan Women in Exile
items.content:
27,846 photographs, 144 countries, and the top prize, worth 6,000 euros, went to a bathroom appliance: the hairdryer. Hairdryers, rather, held aloft at arm’s length by young women who fled Afghanistan. “The Cut” by Silvia Alessi was named Peace Image of the Year 2026 before a packed hall, in the Wappensaal of City Hall, where city councillor Alexandra Rezaei represented the mayor, Michael Ludwig.

A forbidden trade

In power since August 2021, the Taliban have also closed beauty salons to women. It was one of the last trades still open to them, and their hair, incidentally, disappears under the headscarf anyway. What their country refuses them, these young exiles now learn in Pakistan, in classrooms equipped with mirrors, hairdressing tools and mannequins.

Juror Peter-Matthias Gaede summed it up in his tribute: every hairdryer becomes a weapon for self-determination, visibility and the right to choose a profession. The word is strong, perhaps too strong for an image whose charm lies in its lightness. Sand, garnet and rust-coloured headscarves stand out against a grey wall, the cables hang like vines, and the half-masked faces look all the more directly at the camera. The symbolism is a little heavy-handed, but the insolence of the raised arms saves it from slogan. The photographer also received the prize for best single image, 1,000 euros provided by the Austrian Photographic Society (PHG).

In an earlier life, Silvia Alessi styled hair for a living. Born in Brescia in 1975, she worked as a hairdresser for over ten years before discovering photojournalism on a trip to Asia in 2004. She has since worked in Japan, India and Iraq, and been published across most major European countries as well as in Israel and the Philippines. Are there more decisive battlegrounds for women’s rights than the hairdressing salon, the school, the university, the doctor’s surgery? No doubt. But what she uncovered there is anything but trivial, she says: these women hold a tool of empowerment in their hands.

Making peace with the sea

Alongside the top prize, three series also received 1,000 euros each. Antonio Denti, born in Catania in 1972, studied anthropology in London before covering Kosovo, Afghanistan, Iraq, Israel and Gaza for Reuters, then the start of the Arab Spring in Tunisia, natural disasters, contemporary migration and the Pope’s travels. This time he followed, near Rome, African migrant women and their children born in Italy, encouraged to unlearn their fear of water. For them, the Mediterranean remains the memory of a crossing in a makeshift boat, a second desert after the one they had fled.

“I am an intruder into the lives of others,” he says, “and I must at least try, for a few moments, to sense what they themselves are feeling. Photography must be an expression of humanity.” Denti tracked down some of these women years after their crossing, and followed them from their homes to the beach and out into the water, capturing moments of relaxation and daring, but also faces where the fear had not quite lifted. Making peace with the sea is the project, and the series is called “Il Mare in Mezzo” (“The Sea In Between”).

Aleksandra Kossowska, 48, based in Warsaw and co-founder of the Poleczki.art centre, travelled to Sebeta, Ethiopia, to photograph blind and visually impaired children in black and white. They live in a spartan shelter, in cramped shared dormitories, far from their families, yet surrounded by care and driven by the desire to achieve independence in the world of the sighted. The photographer scattered clouds of stars over the portraits, then perforated the prints by hand so that the children could touch them too. “The world touches us when we touch it,” she says. Making blindness visible is impossible, she admits herself, and these stars are its translation. One may wonder whether they illuminate or embellish.

Wings among the ruins

A peace prize for a childhood in Gaza: the pairing is surprising at first. Yet Mahmoud Abu Hamda, 36, a former photography lecturer at the University of Gaza, shows children laughing, a boy playing the violin, swings set up amid the rubble. According to the prize organisers, the photographer was displaced, then injured when the Israeli Air Force bombed a high-rise building, and he documented hunger while starving himself. Perhaps he sought out these carefree moments, he told Magnum, because amid so much misery he too sometimes needed a place to rest. “To breathe.” Magnum has already published his work, which has been shown in Amsterdam, among other places, and won a Lucia Award in 2023.

For the Childrens Peace Image of the Year 2026, the prize went to Sesilia Shainidze, 11, from Batumi, Georgia. Her mother works as an insurance agent, her father as an offshore engineer, and her own camera is currently broken. For “My Family”, she staged a tableau at her grandmother’s house with her grandmother, uncle, aunt, cousins and dog, an idea entirely her own. She also enjoys painting and travelling, and mostly photographs animals, especially her dog, whom she raised herself. She took home 1,000 euros.

Last Thursday, in Vienna, actor Cornelius Obonya, honorary ambassador of UNICEF Austria, delivered the keynote and devoted his speech to the invasion of Ukraine. He closed with a wish: “May the message conveyed in and through your photographs lead to better news from the war-torn regions of this planet.”

One may regret that an awards list surrounded by so many speeches lets the cause speak louder than the writing. But the prize’s initiator, Lois Lammerhuber, had set the frame in his address: “peace is not the absence of war, but something I would describe as a ‘life well lived’.”

The 2026 winners and shortlist are presented on the Global Peace Photo Award website.

items.title: Colin Dodgson, Saturation to Breaking Point
items.content:
IN IMAGES

Colin Dodgson, Saturation to Breaking Point

With Earthquake Weather, his debut monograph published by Loose Joints, the American photographer casts fragility, mortality and the everyday as allegories of a saturated world.


By Guénola Pellen. Photos by Colin Dodgson.

When he is not shooting campaigns for Dior, Gucci and Louis Vuitton in Vogue, W Magazine or The New York Times Style Magazine, Colin Dodgson pursues a photography entirely his own, printing his work by hand in the darkroom. In these images, his eye carries what his publisher calls “the dual inheritance of two formative disciplines”: “a surfer’s responsiveness to shifting conditions”.

Earthquake Weather dances along the faultlines between typology and sprawl: thumbed, dog-eared book pages worn soft by use; contemporary memento mori that turn to the flesh and its impermanence; plastic water bottles left on Japanese roadsides. So many figures of a precarious existence, gathered without hierarchy or imposed narrative, in burnished, copper tones.

Without warning, the sequence drifts towards a darker register. Fentanyl bottles appear, lined neatly in a row. Atmospheric CO2 readings insert themselves between the silhouettes and the worn books, alongside extracts from his collaborations with the World Land Trust — a British charity dedicated to protecting threatened natural habitats — across areas of ecological importance. The tenor of an uncertain age seeps in, uncommented upon, by simple contiguity.

What organizes Earthquake Weather is accumulation — not as rhetorical device, but as condition of the world. The book explores “the way we accumulate: in knowledge, within our bodies, through consumption, against entropy.” The images work as fugues, reacting across the page: beauty and ruin coexist.

Dodgson’s photography chases what “both hides and reveals itself within the same blink of an eye.” He has slipped into its pages photographs of volumes leafed through and annotated — and his own book might follow suit, becoming, through use, one of the photographs it contains.




Earthquake Weather by Colin Dodgson is published by Loose Joints, edited by Sarah Chaplin Espenon. 88 pages, 60 colour plates. €46.

items.title: Amadou Fall: Faces of Nouadhibou
items.content:
IN IMAGES

Amadou Fall: Faces of Nouadhibou

Pattern is presented as the first book devoted to a Mauritanian studio photographer: Amadou Fall, who portrayed the people of Nouadhibou at his Studio Grand Fall from the 1960s onward.

 

By Gaia Squarci. Photographs by Amadou Fall

“Pushing open the door of Studio Grand Fall meant leaving the street behind. The dust stayed outside. The noise too,” writes photographer Adrien Tache. Amadou Fall’s son entrusted Tache with bringing the archive to life, after decades of leaving it untouched. Nomadic families, city dwellers, Spanish migrants, merchants and officials all sat in front of his lens. Together they form a collective portrait of an Atlantic port where North Africa, West Africa and Europe met.

The clothes in Fall’s portraits tell that same story. For a long time, Mauritanian dress favoured plain or indigo-dyed cottons. Then came wax prints: cottons whose bold, colourful patterns are created by using wax to resist the dye. Dutch and British factories first produced them in imitation of Indonesian batik, intending to sell them in Asia. It was in West Africa, however, that they found their public during the nineteenth century, as traders and their customers gave each motif a name of their own, linked to marriage, wealth, migration or independence.

Rather than replacing traditional garments, wax cloth was integrated into existing ways of dressing, and by the 1960s it had become a sign of modernity and aspiration. That same cloth now binds the book: each copy is covered in a different wax fabric printed in West Africa, echoing the patterns some of the sitters could have been wearing.

 

The book Pattern is published by Fraglich Publishing and available for 35 Euro.

items.title: In Brussels, Photographers Set the Sun-Drawing Alight
items.content:
Two hundred years ago, Nicéphore Niépce set a tin plate before his Burgundian window and waited. Hours passed; light did its work. No brush, no chisel — only the chemical reaction of Judean bitumen under the sun, and the world inscribed itself, unaided, onto a sensitive surface. His contemporaries called it the “sun-drawing,” with the same wonder that would seize, seventy years later, the audiences of the Lumière brothers watching their first cinematic projection: a train pulling into the station at La Ciotat.

In the age of artificial intelligence, images can still be born without a camera. The “this-has-been” so dear to the philosopher of the image Roland Barthes, that certainty that some real thing had once stood before a lens, no longer holds. In 2026, faces, landscapes and hyperrealistic scenes are conjured from nothing. It is within this great technological trembling that the Cnap and the Hangar — a Brussels art centre dedicated to contemporary photography — commissioned twenty artists: fifteen French, five Belgian, selected through an open call. Neither nostalgia nor ritual celebration, but a shared experiment in what the medium might yet become.

The return to origins begins with matter. Brussels-based artist Julie Calbert recovers the chemical residues of analogue photography, reintroduces them into the laboratory and sets them back in motion. From the photosensitive surface emerge phenomena of formation, propagation and erosion that she calls “unstable cartographies.” The image arrives on its own, with an almost organic autonomy: photography reclaims its original condition — a chemical reaction left to itself — and the artist reclaims hers, as a witness who guides without commanding.

Others surrender to time. French photographer Marie Bovo shoots at night, on a large-format camera, with exposures lasting up to nine hours, lit by nothing but the moon and the stars. Her “Forêts d’Hypnos” series stretch from the mimosa groves of the Tanneron to the hills of Tipaza, in Algeria, where vegetation has overgrown ancient Muslim graves from the colonial era. The night sky is streaked by the luminous trails of satellites while the trees hold centuries of buried memory, “immobile condensations of movements perceptible only through duration.”

More radical still: the renunciation of the gesture itself. In a valley of the Haute Maurienne, in the Alps, photographer and documentary filmmaker Michel Slomka scatters a constellation of camera traps and surrenders the shutter to the forest, the wind, the seasons, the passage of wolves. These devices, he notes, are “less surveillance cameras than small, motionless witnesses.” He has simply “tried to reduce the human footprint to a minimum” so that the animal’s footprint leaves, in the end, a photographic one. The work poses the question: who, exactly, makes the photograph?

It remained to make the dead speak. French artist Stéphanie Solinas unearthed eighteen portraits of young women from the nineteenth century on the American West Coast, driven by a single question: “What do you have to say to me today?” Drawing on a chain of tools running from mediumship to artificial intelligence, the installation “Une sorte de bordel” (2026), on the second floor of the Hangar, conjures from these pioneers a contemporary and animated lineage. A table called “diseuse” — fortune-teller — fitted with a tactile silicone hand, invites the visitor somewhere between oracle and dating app. Algorithms have replaced the ouija board.

On the floor below, the spectacular installation by visual artist François Bellabas rises like a monolith: a body-scale screen pours out an abstract, sonorous matter from which an embryo of his double surfaces, sharpens, dissolves, is reborn. The artist fed an algorithm on his own images, then “cut the process” at the moment when forms are still abstract, before the machine could complete its invention. “Our images, turned into fuel for machines, are computed in alien times”: by intercepting that stream, he grants his digital double “a space in which to take form.” The longer the visitor lingers, the more the double solidifies. It is the viewer who ends up being watched.

The same tension — between the photographer and his machinic double — inhabits the work of Sébastien Van Malleghem. A seasoned photojournalist with fifteen years of social documentary practice in black and white across northern Europe, he pivots with “V”(2026) toward colour, toward the light of Madeira and the Azores, and toward the machine. His prints on baryta paper hang in dialogue with a film generated entirely by AI from his own photographs. “Where photography offers a space of calm and beauty, its animated double provokes a diffuse unease,” he notes. A way of anchoring the living in paper, and holding anxiety at arm’s length.

Laurent Millet, meanwhile, seeks weight in the places where photography resists. “I nearly gave up photography several times because of its thinness, which I could find unbearable,” he confides. His theatres of illusion and scale models, built from nineteenth-century techniques now accessible to all, set a sculptural density against the medium’s transparency. The more objective an image becomes, he argues, the more it operates as a window that erases itself: he demands that it be “something very present, concrete, that pushes back against the eye.”

“To speak of the Bicentenary,” says Delphine Dumont, director of the Hangar, “is necessarily to interrogate the time in which we find ourselves.” The time of history, of creation, of institutions? Perhaps above all, she suggests, “the time proper to art: a time that escapes calendars, but leaves traces.” The poet Théophile Gautier wrote as much in 1864, in a phrase the exhibition catalogue exhumes as its epigraph: “The sun is tireless and photographers will not succeed in exhausting its patience.” Two hundred years after the Point de vue du Gras, other suns are rising over Brussels.

“Reinventing Photography” is on view at the Hangar, Brussels, until 20 December 2026.

The Hangar publishes 200 Years Later: Photography Reinvented by Five Belgian Artists, a leporello devoted to the five Belgian artists in the exhibition — Hangar Edition (2026).

The CNAP and Éditions Poursuite (Arles) co-publish Réinventer la photographie, a book bringing together invited texts and an essay by Jean-Christophe Bailly on the fifteen French artists exhibited (2026).

items.title: Punk, Anonymous and Feminist: the Anti-Selfie According to K8 Hardy
items.content:
IN IMAGES

Punk, Anonymous and Feminist: the Anti-Selfie According to K8 Hardy

American artist K8 Hardy takes over MoMA with “Position Series”, featured in the group exhibition “Taking Back Our Space,” alongside the publication of Positions by MACK, which brings together the fifty photographs of the series for the first time.

By Guénola Pellen. Photos by K8 Hardy.

Rooted in second-wave feminism’s claim that the female body is a site of political struggle, K8 Hardy transmutes that legacy into a deliberately unruly, genre-defying practice, playing with the codes of pop culture as much as she detonates them. A founding member of the queer feminist collective LTTR, she weaponizes “bad taste” to dissect systems of consumption. Long before Instagram, she was already staging herself to subvert the codes of capitalism and patriarchy. “I love to ruin something nice.”

“Position Series” (2007-2012) grows from that impulse. K8 Hardy mobilizes her sister, mannequins, and her own body — dressed in eccentric clothes, wigs, and makeup — to embody figures that spill beyond any normative categorization of identity and gender expression. Each portrait is printed vertically, in magazine format, by mimicry as much as by subversive intent. MACK gathers the fifty photographs, expanded with unseen images, alongside a text by Brontez Purnell, a leading figure of the American queer literary scene and author of 100 Boyfriends.

In the darkroom, K8 Hardy methodically sabotages her own images: cutting negatives, taping them back together, layering them, deliberately choosing the failed shot. “The interventions become interference,” she says. Everything is aimed at unmasking photography as construction rather than fixed truth, at short-circuiting that moment of belief in an image. “It wasn’t about getting the shot, it was about making it.”

The series’ wardrobe follows the same logic of friction. “I see style as just another tool on my tool belt,” says K8 Hardy, drawing exclusively from thrift stores, never conceding an inch to luxury or designer labels. The looks generate a deliberate dissonance with their settings — a cafeteria, a chain-link fence, a floral armchair — captured across travels through Chile, Texas, Italy, and Argentina. The goal? “Stay common, but peculiar.”

In the lineage of surrealist trailblazer Claude Cahun, of Marianne Wex, who catalogued gendered body language, and of Coco Fusco, performer and critic of colonial representation, K8 Hardy constructs figures that are neither icons nor quite anonymous in their representation. Her model, she says with a laugh, is “a no one who is someone.” A concept our own era has since caught up with. “Now it’s impossible to look at this series outside the regime of the selfie,” she acknowledges.

The exhibition “Taking Back Our Space: Photographic Perspectives” runs at MoMA, New York, through May 2, 2027.

Positions (2026) by K8 Hardy is published by MACK (128 pp., $85), in a limited edition of 1,000 signed copies.

items.title: Jordan Rossi: “Joy Is Political in Its Own Way”
items.content:
Jordan Rossi has always walked a fine line. British with Italian and Irish roots, he shoots the London queer scene and luxury brand campaigns with equal conviction, never appearing to betray either. His gaze turns fashion photography — vivid, often irreverent — into a tool for intimate and social portraiture. With a single obsession: catching the moment his subjects drop the mask.

The title of your first exhibition, “Homecoming”, speaks of both return and belonging. What does that word mean to you?

Jordan Rossi: “Homecoming” felt like the only possible title. I grew up between two cultures, Italian and Irish, but I was born and raised in London — so I’ve always had a slightly complicated relationship with the idea of “home”. I don’t think I’ve ever felt entirely one thing or another.

Bringing this body of work to Italy feels like closing a circle. These photographs cover nearly a decade of my life, made in London, Los Angeles and elsewhere. Bringing them here, to a country that is part of my identity and my family, feels very personal. But with time, “home” has become less geographical for me. It’s the people you surround yourself with, the communities you find, and eventually the space you create for yourself. In that sense, “Homecoming” is as much about where I am now as it is about where I came from.

You have shot the queer community of East London just as much as campaigns for Rolls-Royce. Are these two worlds not in conflict, and how do you move between them?

Jordan Rossi: I’ve never really seen them as being in conflict. The scale, budgets and expectations might be completely different, but ultimately I’m still interested in the same things: people, character, and creating a world around them.

I also don’t think queer artists should have to exist solely within queer spaces. I can photograph someone in a club in East London and then direct a campaign for a global brand — both can still contain my point of view. If anything, moving between those worlds matters to me. The experiences and communities that shaped me inevitably find their way into the commercial work, and the resources of the commercial world feed back into my personal work. I don’t want either side of my career to exist in isolation from the other.

Your photography is generally described as queer, committed, rooted in fashion and portraiture. What would you add about your work and where it has taken you?

Jordan Rossi: I’d probably add that there’s a sense of performance running through a lot of it. I’m interested in the version of ourselves that we construct for the camera: fashion, sexuality, masculinity, femininity, celebrity, glamour. Portraiture can document somebody, but it can also give them permission to become something else for a moment.

Over the past decade that has taken me into very different rooms — from emerging performers and people within the queer community to actors, musicians, fashion houses and global brands. I’ve photographed people I admired long before I ever picked up a camera professionally, which still feels slightly surreal. But when I look across the work now, what interests me isn’t necessarily who is famous and who isn’t. It’s that the same curiosity runs through all of it. I’m drawn to people who have a strong sense of who they are — or who are in the process of discovering it.

You are a photographer, a filmmaker and a creative director all at once. Concretely, how do you hold those three roles together?

Jordan Rossi: What I’ve realised over time is that every time I’ve added another discipline, it has changed the way I approach everything else.

There are instincts and skills that move between them. Photography made me much more aware of the relationship you build with the person in front of your camera. It can be incredibly intimate — just two people trying to find something together. Learning how to create that trust changed the way I worked with performers when I returned to directing. In the same way, years of filmmaking and creative direction have made me think differently about still images. I’m rarely just thinking about whether something looks beautiful; I’m thinking about the world around it, the character, the emotion, and what the image is trying to say.

That’s ultimately how I hold all three together: they’ve become part of the same visual language. I’m constantly taking things I’ve learned in one area into another, often without consciously realizing it. I’m less interested now in whether something makes me a photographer, director or creative director — and more interested in finding the best way to tell the story in front of me.

In your work, you have chosen to show the joy of the LGBTQIA+ community rather than its trauma. Do you feel a particular responsibility towards that community — and if so, what does it look like?

Jordan Rossi: Absolutely — although I try not to let that responsibility turn into the idea that there is one correct way to represent a community as enormous and varied as ours.

For a long time, so many LGBTQIA+ stories were framed through tragedy, rejection or suffering. Those stories are real and important, but they aren’t the entirety of queer life. I became much more interested in photographing the other side of it: friendship, sex, humor, beauty, ridiculousness, confidence, intimacy and joy. Not as a denial of the difficult things, but because those things are also political in their own way. There is power in seeing queer people simply having a brilliant time, taking up space, being desired rather than apologising for being there.

My responsibility is really to the people in front of my camera. I want them to feel they have agency in how they’re represented, and I want the work to come from being part of a community rather than looking at it from the outside. I don’t think my job is to speak for LGBTQIA+ people. It’s to contribute my perspective to a much bigger, messier and more interesting story.

Jordan Rossi’s show “Homecoming” is on view at Galleria Rubin, Milan (Italy), from September 22 to October 3rd, 2026.

items.title: Susan kae Grant: Sweet Dreams Are Made of This
items.content:
IN IMAGES

Susan kae Grant: Sweet Dreams Are Made of This

American photographer Susan kae Grant has made dreams her material and her photographic territory. Night Journey, published by MW Editions, is the culmination of a life’s work: a sumptuous and haunting volume, in black and white, crafted with the precision of a haute couturière of the unconscious.

By Guénola Pellen. Photos by Susan kae Grant.

Susan kae Grant grew up in a small town in Wisconsin. A shy and silent child, she expressed herself by drawing, writing, and making collages. Alfred Hitchcock and Rod Serling, creator of the anthology series The Twilight Zone, served as her compass: “the way they created mystery came through tormented theatrical storytelling.”

Trained in photography at the University of Wisconsin-Madison, she went on to teach photography at Texas Woman’s University for thirty-six years. Her artistic lineage connects her to what critic A.D. Coleman called the “directorial mode” — a photography in which the scene is entirely constructed by the photographer, in the tradition of Duane Michals, master of narrative sequence, and Arthur Tress, explorer of childhood dreams and nightmares.

In the 1990s, Susan kae Grant agreed to have electrodes placed on her body and to be awakened during REM sleep to describe aloud what she had just seen. Listening back to the recordings, she discovered a voice she barely recognized, phrases spoken in an in-between state, neither fully asleep nor truly awake. “I realized that these recordings had been made in a different state of consciousness.” The words murmured in the dark — “She’s Afraid to Stop”, “Something Needs Constant Attention”, “We Act Like We Don’t Know One Another” — would become the titles of her photographs.

In her Dallas studio, Susan kae Grant works with a 4×5 camera fitted with a digital back. Rare in contemporary photography, she never photographs her subjects directly — only the shadows they cast. She layers models, props, and floral wire, repositioning directional lights dozens of times, sometimes over months, for a single image.

This shadow theater summons Murnau’s Nosferatu and German Expressionism as much as Plato’s allegory of the cave. “It’s like being inside a gigantic three-dimensional photogram that I can’t fully see until I’m behind the camera,” she explains. “I strive to design sets with a sense of mystery and ambiguity, to provoke a narrative that raises more questions than it answers.”

The silhouettes that populate her images have no faces. These anonymous bodies fall, embrace, reach toward something just out of frame. As essayist Deborah Willis writes in the book’s opening essay titled Mapping the Dream Terrain, these figures “function less as characters than as vessels for sensation and memory,” inviting the viewer to project their own nights onto the page. “The narratives are a representation of a representation, and they exist only in the imagination.”

Founder of The Black Rose Press since 1976, Susan kae Grant has produced twelve limited-edition artist books, held in the collections of the Getty Museum and the Tokyo Photographic Art Museum. Night Journey is their crowning achievement. With its gatefolds, triptychs, and an entire section printed on translucent paper where images layer like strata of memory, the book performs, down to its very design, the logic of the dream.




Night Journey by Susan kae Grant is published by MW Editions and available for $70.

items.content:
IN IMAGES

At the Martin Parr Foundation, the Gothic Next Door

The Martin Parr Foundation presents “Dark Tales: British Documentary and the Gothic,” an exhibition that reminds the viewer what makes an atmosphere distinctively British: a fondness for dark irony, layered emotional depth, and a passion for the absurd.

 

By Gaia Squarci. Cover Photo by Chris Shaw

Curator Isaac Blease drew the selection from over 5,000 prints in the Foundation’s collection, spanning more than 80 years, from the post-war years to the present. Together they build a haunted, playful narrative that shows photography’s power to visualise fear and fascination — proof, as Blease puts it, of the Gothic principle that horror lives closest to the familiar.

 

Rather than impose a single viewpoint, the show lets atmosphere serve as its thread, moving from historical documentation to domestic unease to class, into the rituals of appearance and respectability, where details of style are always an indicator of a deeper message. Fading industrial towns, claustrophobic interiors, and eerie nocturnal scenes recur throughout, in work by Bill Brandt, Anna Fox, Don McCullin, Lee Miller, Chris Shaw, and many others.

The exhibition “Dark Tales: British Documentary and the Gothic” is on view at the Martin Parr Foundation in Bristol, UK, until December 20.

items.title: Denis Boulze and the Sweet Life of Clichés
items.content:
“Images don’t belong to us. Proust’s madeleine is the same for everyone.” Set as the epigraph of Clichés (in French, the word means both a stereotype and a photograph), Denis Boulze’s line has the candor of a confession slipped backstage, between two takes. The photographer knows the recipe, having served it for years in the pages of Vogue, Silhouette and Milk, for Hermès and JM Weston: a face, a hand, a shaft of light, and the reader’s memory does the rest. A proven recipe. On Roxane Moreau’s podcast Dans le bain, recorded on the evening of his first solo exhibition, Denis Boulze readily speaks of his “candy images.” Sweet, then, and a little guilty.

The taste goes back a long way. The son of a photographer, Denis Boulze started as an intern at 16 at Studio Rouchon in Paris, where he later assisted Sarah Moon, Jan Walter, Sofia and Mauro. A tough school, and a lucky draw. In the acknowledgments, he gives his father his due, the man who passed on to him “a taste for the image” and taught him “to see.” The rest reads like a travel journal, since this “beautiful profession,” he writes, “has always been a pretext for me to travel, meet new people and live experiences that have deeply enriched me.” A craftsman’s courtesy, which also salutes his agent, the formidable Florence Moll, and the printers David Dahan and Luis Escudero, thanks to whom color printing has, as the artist puts it, “today become an essential part of my work.”

So why a book? Weariness? Remorse? A big spring cleaning? On his professional profile, Denis Boulze once let out this cry from the heart: “Help, fashion! Seeing the same photographers, the same stylists, the same models over and over, I’m getting a little bored.” Clichés answers with the simplest gesture: opening the archive boxes, cutting, pasting, layering. The bags, the bottles, the logos evaporate. What remains are bodies, gestures, postures. Claire Luna, winner of the 2025 AICA-France Élisabeth Couturier Prize for art criticism, sees in it, in her opening text, “almost a visual coming out,” and extends the metaphor all the way to the closet: the curtain has risen, “but something still lies coiled.”

What you find inside: 16 faces striped with shadow, 16 hands raised as if to stop traffic, a white dove above a red and orange puddle, starfish clinging to an ear. A moodboard? Almost. Denis Boulze works in diptychs and strips, slipping a tab of red or khaki-green paper between two prints, the way one dog-ears a page in a cookbook. A woman’s profile answers an antique plaster head; two long-necked bottles bathe in a day-for-night blue, a Morandi gone to the movies; a transparent dress floats against black, a dry cleaner’s ghost. The painted lips, for their part, are doubled, like a rubber stamp pressed twice (Blumenfeld and Man Ray have been here before).

The strength of the whole lies in its softness. Everything here belongs to reminiscence, a tune hummed without knowing who wrote it, hence the title Claire Luna chose, “Comme une chanson populaire” (Like a Popular Song). Denis Boulze embraces this shared memory, which he also claims for his series “Portrait de famille” (Family Portrait), made every summer in a former chestnut-drying hut in the Cévennes: a series “very dear to me,” he wrote, “although it is unfinished and will probably remain so forever,” meant to preserve “this parenthesis of our lives which, in my opinion, resembles a gentle poetry.” Clichés shares this slow tempo, like a family album whose members happen to be strangers.

Designed by Line Célo and printed by LONGO in Bolzano, the book has the restraint of a portfolio laid on a table at a festival portfolio review. Generous white space, airy sequences, color used sparingly and all the more precious for it. Some plates read like a catalog of forms, plaster spheres and half-moons in a Bauhaus vein; others keep a touch of glamour that Denis Boulze owns without false modesty. One could see this as a limitation. One could also read it as a form of honesty: the photographer lays out his alphabet, worn letters included, and leaves readers to recognize their own words in it.

Which leaves the question of authorship. To whom does a hand resting on a cheek belong, an eye under makeup, a glass of milk on a dark table? To everyone, answers the epigraph. To whoever looks, the book corrects. Denis Boulze has known this since childhood, and closes his acknowledgments with his father, thanked for a lifelong lesson: “the importance of looking and cultivating my eye.”

Denis Boulze’s Clichés, with a text by Claire Luna, is self-published and available for €40. To buy the book, contact Denis Boulze directly via his Instagram account.

items.title: Two Images Are Better Than One
items.content:
IN IMAGES

Two Images Are Better Than One

In Frozen Features, American photographer and publisher Jason Fulford overlays his negatives at random. From each collision emerges a third image, forging its own syntax.

By Guénola Pellen. Photos by Jason Fulford.

A knife plunged into a white table, its shadow stretching long as an accusation, and around it, scattered like coins on a counter, watch faces stripped of their hands. Welcome to Frozen Features: a book where every image is already double, where meaning surfaces in the gap, sharp and immediate, before any explanation.

Jason Fulford holds ten thousand digitized negatives, thirty years of images kept in envelopes, boxed, stored in a cabinet. Last year, he began overlaying them at random, two negatives at a time, to see what their meeting might produce. From roughly a thousand pairs generated by chance, he kept a few hundred, then spent two days with Sarah Chaplin Espenon, editor at Loose Joints, whittling them down to fifty-four: purely intuitive work.

Only the combinations that “sing” survive. Charles Goslin, his graphic design professor, used to collect obituaries from The New York Times featuring people who had led double lives, two improbable existences fused into one. He asked his students to distill that duality into a single logo. Jason Fulford never stopped practicing that exercise.

For the photographer, two images placed side by side alter each other: from their encounter emerges an additional layer of meaning. Ferdinand de Saussure, the father of modern linguistics, put it this way: the value of a sign arises not from its own content, but from its difference from all the others.

A man seen from behind paints a madonna in watercolor against the New Mexico sky: without the straight road stretching beneath his brush, without the arid desert around him, the figure is nothing. With it, she becomes an apparition. Jason Fulford forges morphemes, minimal units whose meaning stays suspended, waiting for encounter.

Frozen Features opens with a line from American photographer Barbara Morgan, written in 1942: “Modern life is photomontage. In our thoughts and feelings, the images vital to us move together, skipping over the factual detail.” Jason Fulford takes her at her word, then goes further: he surrenders syntax to chance in order to surface the grammar buried beneath conscious thought. 

TThese photographs each existed independently, made across thirty years of practice, yet were never intended to meet. In his address to the reader, Jason Fulford writes: “A metaphysical slot machine scoured my subconscious & fed it back to me, two memories at a time.” A fragmented face in a rearview mirror while a freight train barrels past in the background: two moments that never crossed paths now share the same second, and time ceases to be chronological. It becomes stratigraphic.

“The only way for them to last is for them to never fully be resolved,” says Jason Fulford — and one thinks of what American art historian Benjamin Buchloh wrote about Gerhard Richter’s paintings: vexations, puzzles that seem to promise a solution yet resist every attempt to reach one.

Roland Barthes, the French theorist of the image and founding father of modern semiology, called punctum that detail which pricks in a photograph and wounds, in the literal sense: a puncture, a breach in the gaze. Jason Fulford makes images with a double punctum: a toy dinosaur skeleton dissolving into the pink facade of a building at night, two simultaneous wounds contaminating each other. It is, as Loose Joints puts it, work that is “felt before it’s understood.”

Jason Fulford puts it plainly: “I always try to make work that the reader finishes.” And so Frozen Features is not a closed book: it is a half-written score, a sentence missing its verb. This is where the reader comes in. Two images are better than one, granted. But two images plus a gaze: that’s a complete sentence. Yours to make.

 

Frozen Features by Jason Fulford is published by Loose Joints, 104 pages, 54 color plates, $68.

items.title: Zone i Tousles Photography
items.content:
“There will be grain and seeds of gazes, music, strange processes, the LUX Tour and of course, the refreshment bar and local catering.” Monica Santos and Mat Jacob, the founders of Zone i, had announced it, and they kept their word. There was more: encounters, debate, swims in the river and live music.

As the first rehearsals of ABAL, a choir of Occitan polyphonic songs, ring out, a foghorn soon answers from the horizon. A rallying call goes out across the grounds: “Meet in the barn, the Photo Jam Session is about to start!” For the third year running, the Photo Jam Sessions invite photographers of all backgrounds and ages to present their work as a short projection. “The original idea was to evolve the portfolio review, where you find yourself face to face with maestros who assess your work,” explains Mat Jacob. The aim is to restore a form of horizontality with an audience, and to spark emulation, debate, advice and remarks. Mat Jacob sums it up simply: “It can be very enriching to be criticized with kindness.”

While some projects are already far along, accomplished or even finished, most are still in progress or being shown to an audience for the first time. Practices intersect: documentary photography, experiments, video, editing or more singular technical processes. From Jean Puybaraud’s work on the genocide of the Yaghan people to Eve Campestrini’s series exploring the imaginary of a collective of farmers committed to the ecological transition, the subjects differ, but the social and environmental concerns echo each other.

Questioning the territory

From May to October, Zone i deploys a multidisciplinary program of exhibitions, talks, workshops, concerts and artistic projects around image, environment and education. The festival found refuge nearly ten years ago at the Moulin de la Fontaine, a former place of production and gatherings that is now a cultural laboratory dedicated to photography. Just as the miller once worked grain with the force of water, photographers now shape the grain of images there, capturing light, time and the stories of the living world. With “Graines et grain de regards” (Seeds and Grain of Gazes), five photographers from the area are invited to share one of their series as a carte blanche, in the Moulin de la Fontaine and along its banks.

In her series “Récit d’architecture ordinaire” (Tale of Ordinary Architecture), photographer Anne Piégu shows the traces of a rural world that is disappearing, along with the stories of those who lived in it. We meet Jacqueline, who married at 22 and joined her husband on the family farm. She was the one who milked the cows. And Colette, who arrived with her daughters 60 years ago. She was the first to have a house built in a small valley, facing the cellars of a village with a winemaking tradition.

Through these stories, Anne recounts the transformation of the landscapes and ways of life that shaped her childhood. Her gaze goes beyond the rural world, because everywhere territories are changing, landscapes are shifting and certain ways of living are vanishing. What remains is photography, the only medium able to preserve the traces of what no longer exists. Beno Lelong bears witness to this with “Notes sur une ville qui n’existe plus” (Notes on a City That No Longer Exists). For several years, the artist roamed Nantes, living in squats and empty houses among other places. His images archive the remnants of an alternative city, the city of his memories, and also of a way of life that has since disappeared.

Between tribute and legacy

Sometimes photographs themselves become traces to be found. This year, some of the exhibitions bring back gazes that time had covered over. The first is Jean-Pierre’s, through the series “Jean-Pierre, Béquilles et Beautiful People” (Jean-Pierre, Crutches and Beautiful People), presented by Séba Lallemand. Jean-Pierre was homeless in Paris when Séba met him in the early 2000s, while working on a commission for an agency. They talked about photography, Jean-Pierre confessed his wish to try the medium, and Séba handed him his loaded Olympus MJU-II.

A curious trade followed. Séba developed the images, they arranged to meet “on a bench opposite the Fouquet’s on the Champs-Elysées, his headquarters,” and Séba showed him the prints. In the harsh light of the flash, Jean-Pierre captured the wealthy districts, the jet set and its share of pomp, luxury and glitter. He also captured the street, the pavement, the misery and those faces we pass every day without really looking at them. “People looked at him, the tramp, and he looked at people, the rich, the lost night owls, the poor.” Jean-Pierre got so caught up in the game that he bought himself small disposable Kodaks. “What was incredible is that he was as hooked on photography as he was on alcohol.”

The selection presented at Zone i is drawn from 47 rolls of film. There would be no 48th, as Jean-Pierre died before. Séba describes Jean-Pierre as having “the appearance of the celestial Parisian tramp, proud, drunk, with a smashed nose and greasy hair.” In the only image of him on show, he appears with eyes half closed, blinded by the sun, hair disheveled and cigarette hanging from his lips, a bling-bling chain (surely fake) around his neck. Of his identity, nothing is known: “he stayed very discreet about his past.” All that remains is his gaze, which transfigures the daily life of millions of people. A testimony free of judgment and a last thumbing of the nose at humanist street photography, with a Kodak snap.

On the top floor of the mill, a second photographer is pulled from the dust of the attic. Forgotten after publishing 14 books, Christian Louis sees his work rediscovered after his death. It reveals a photography halfway between documentary and poetic narrative, one that seeks not the event but what happens beside it, in the interstices of reality. In chiaroscuro, he captures the jolts of a France in the midst of change, between industrial decline, urban expansion and new ways of life.

Out of frame

A “clack” rings out in the middle of the field. It is the machine of Thomas Ozoux, the Photocotype: “an old photocopier to which I added a magnifying glass lens and that I covered with the panels of an old wardrobe.” It sits enthroned at the center of the Zone i labyrinth, a work made of around 100 old doors and recycled mirrors. Since childhood, Thomas has tortured his films and tinkered with his cameras. He continues to bend reality with his inventions. His long exposures recall those of the daguerreotype, while his “failures” and “monsters” reveal another side of reality. His photocotypes are also on show at the Moulin de la Fontaine.

At the exit of the labyrinth, another “clack” rings out. This time it is an air rifle. After having your portrait taken, what better than to take a shot at a portrait? That is what Mat Jacob’s shooting stand offers, soberly titled “Innocentes photos de merde” (Innocent Crappy Photos). A tribute to the images that regularly appear before the court of public opinion and suffer, too, the violence of technology. Fire!

And to restore some calm to all this, nothing beats soothing your heart by leaving with the photograph of one of your own pulses. The experience is made possible by the laboratory of the Trigone team, a member of the Lux network, which parks its caravan at Zone i for the bicentenary of photography. By bringing the electrical pulse of a heartbeat into dialogue with the movement of photons on a sensitive surface, the photographic process here transfigures one’s own heart into an image. These devices all remind us that Zone i remains above all a sensory experience, more than just a festival, and reflect the place’s determination, voiced by Mat Jacob: “to bring photography to life, whether it’s serious or not.”

items.title: Black Cowboys Are Back in the Arena
items.content:
IN IMAGES

Black Cowboys Are Back in the Arena

Two years after the success of Eight Seconds: Black Rodeo Culture, Damiani releases a new edition featuring 91 previously unpublished photographs, with a foreword by James Pickens Jr., Grey’s Anatomy actor and rodeo devotee.

 

 

By Guénola Pellen. Photos by Ivan McClellan.

Present on the ranches of the American West since the end of the Civil War, where they made up no less than a quarter of the workforce, Black cowboys have long been rendered invisible by Hollywood and the American national myth. A distortion that photographer Ivan McClellan has been dismantling for ten years, from the dusty arenas of Oklahoma to the red clay lands of Texas.

“We see the faces. The joy. The color. The pageantry. The fellowship. We witness triumph and pain, history and legacy — but above all, celebration,” writes Pickens Jr., an avid rider and organiser of team roping events across Southern California. “This is a Western lifestyle uniquely shaped by the Black cowboy and cowgirl experience.”

“It showed me how vital the Black cowboy’s story is to the true history — and mythology — of the American West,” writes Pickens Jr. in Eight Seconds: Legacy in Motion, recalling his first Black rodeo in New York City forty years ago. “That experience changed my perspective. It reshaped my understanding of what it really means to be a cowboy.” It took a photographer from Portland to give the American West back its true color.




Eight Seconds: Legacy in Motion by Ivan McClellan. Foreword by James Pickens Jr. Damiani Books, 112 pages, 91 color photographs. $50
